tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.name: helm_list
tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

all_namespaces.description: If true, lists all Helm releases in all namespaces ignoring the namespace argument (Optional)

namespace.description: Namespace to list Helm releases from (Optional, all namespaces if not provided)

tools.name: helm_uninstall
tools.description: Uninstall a Helm release in the current or provided namespace

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Deployment name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container port/security: matched stable (containerPort: 80, no additional securityContext)

- Updated Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Ports unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching the existing setup

Result
- With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 in engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 across stable and canary.

Optional quick checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

If you want to revert to 100% stable, I can switch the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Deployed canary
  - Deployment name: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container port/security: matched stable (containerPort: 80, no additional securityContext)

- Updated Service
  - Service: recommendation-engine (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Ports unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), matching the existing setup

Result
- With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 in engine-v2-1, the Service will distribute traffic roughly 50/50 across stable and canary.

Optional quick checks
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy engine-v2-0 engine-v2-1
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get pods -l app=recommendation-engine -o wide
- kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine

If you want to revert to 100% stable, I can switch the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

Steps.message:
Done. Here’s what I found and fixed:

- Root cause: The container was overriding the entrypoint with /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff.
- Fix applied: Removed the custom command and args so the container uses the image’s default entrypoint (nginx). Also set containerPort 8080 for clarity with the nginx-unprivileged image.
- Current status: Deployment app in crashloop-test is Available with 1/1 replicas Ready. The new pod is Running.

If you intended to run a custom startup command, let me know the correct command/args and I can update the deployment accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC unbound, blocking scheduling.

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it with a valid StorageClass: standard (provisioner rancher.io/local-path). No data was lost since the PVC had no volume yet.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc has been dynamically provisioned.
- Pod homepage-pod is now Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane and Ready.

If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that or create a StorageClass named sc to match your original spec.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC unbound, blocking scheduling.

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it with a valid StorageClass: standard (provisioner rancher.io/local-path). No data was lost since the PVC had no volume yet.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc has been dynamically provisioned.
- Pod homepage-pod is now Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane and Ready.

If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that or create a StorageClass named sc to match your original spec.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". That kept the PVC unbound, blocking scheduling.

What I changed
- Deleted the Pending PVC and recreated it with a valid StorageClass: standard (provisioner rancher.io/local-path). No data was lost since the PVC had no volume yet.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc has been dynamically provisioned.
- Pod homepage-pod is now Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane and Ready.

If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that or create a StorageClass named sc to match your original spec.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause:
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and your liveness/readiness probes were checking custom paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80. That caused connection refused and the pod never became Ready. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports include 8080.
  - Liveness and readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080 (so in-cluster clients can still use port 80 via the Service).

Current status:
- New pod is healthy and Ready: webapp-b8996969f-lfhzs.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.33:8080.
- The previous failing pod from the old ReplicaSet will terminate as the rollout completes.

How to test (from your machine):
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access without port-forwarding, I can set up an Ingress/Route or a LoadBalancer Service—let me know your preferred hostname or exposure method.

namespace/orders created

deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause:
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and your liveness/readiness probes were checking custom paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80. That caused connection refused and the pod never became Ready. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports include 8080.
  - Liveness and readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080 (so in-cluster clients can still use port 80 via the Service).

Current status:
- New pod is healthy and Ready: webapp-b8996969f-lfhzs.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.33:8080.
- The previous failing pod from the old ReplicaSet will terminate as the rollout completes.

How to test (from your machine):
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access without port-forwarding, I can set up an Ingress/Route or a LoadBalancer Service—let me know your preferred hostname or exposure method.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause:
- The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (not 80), and your liveness/readiness probes were checking custom paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80. That caused connection refused and the pod never became Ready. The Service was also targeting port 80.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Container ports include 8080.
  - Liveness and readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - Port 80 now targets container port 8080 (so in-cluster clients can still use port 80 via the Service).

Current status:
- New pod is healthy and Ready: webapp-b8996969f-lfhzs.
- Service endpoints are populated: 10.244.0.33:8080.
- The previous failing pod from the old ReplicaSet will terminate as the rollout completes.

How to test (from your machine):
- kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you need external access without port-forwarding, I can set up an Ingress/Route or a LoadBalancer Service—let me know your preferred hostname or exposure method.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- No endpoints: The Service selector didn’t match the pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Endpoints/EndpointSlice initially showed none
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), while the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Verified inside the pod: default.conf has listen 8080

Fix applied
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment/pods)
  - ports: port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (keeps client-facing 80, routes to pod 8080)

Current state (post-fix)
- Endpoints present:
  - 10.244.0.34:8080 backing Service web/nginx
- Pod running and nginx started normally

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  kubectl -n web run tmp-curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -it --rm -- curl -sS -I http://nginx/
  You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). If you were trying to reach it from outside the cluster, expose it via one of:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    Then kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide to see the nodePort
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress (if an Ingress controller is installed). Example:
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Ingress
    metadata:
      name: nginx
      namespace: web
    spec:
      rules:
      - host: your.host.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

Summary
Root causes were a label mismatch (app=web vs app=nginx) and wrong targetPort (80 vs 8080). I corrected the Service to select app=nginx and route port 80 to targetPort 8080. Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- No endpoints: The Service selector didn’t match the pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Endpoints/EndpointSlice initially showed none
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), while the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Verified inside the pod: default.conf has listen 8080

Fix applied
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment/pods)
  - ports: port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (keeps client-facing 80, routes to pod 8080)

Current state (post-fix)
- Endpoints present:
  - 10.244.0.34:8080 backing Service web/nginx
- Pod running and nginx started normally

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  kubectl -n web run tmp-curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -it --rm -- curl -sS -I http://nginx/
  You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). If you were trying to reach it from outside the cluster, expose it via one of:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    Then kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide to see the nodePort
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress (if an Ingress controller is installed). Example:
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Ingress
    metadata:
      name: nginx
      namespace: web
    spec:
      rules:
      - host: your.host.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

Summary
Root causes were a label mismatch (app=web vs app=nginx) and wrong targetPort (80 vs 8080). I corrected the Service to select app=nginx and route port 80 to targetPort 8080. outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- No endpoints: The Service selector didn’t match the pods.
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Endpoints/EndpointSlice initially showed none
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), while the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Verified inside the pod: default.conf has listen 8080

Fix applied
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment/pods)
  - ports: port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (keeps client-facing 80, routes to pod 8080)

Current state (post-fix)
- Endpoints present:
  - 10.244.0.34:8080 backing Service web/nginx
- Pod running and nginx started normally

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- Run a quick test pod and curl the service:
  kubectl -n web run tmp-curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 --restart=Never -it --rm -- curl -sS -I http://nginx/
  You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Notes on external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (in-cluster only). If you were trying to reach it from outside the cluster, expose it via one of:
  - NodePort:
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
    Then kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide to see the nodePort
  - LoadBalancer (if your cluster supports it):
    kubectl -n web patch svc nginx -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'
  - Ingress (if an Ingress controller is installed). Example:
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Ingress
    metadata:
      name: nginx
      namespace: web
    spec:
      rules:
      - host: your.host.example.com
        http:
          paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: nginx
                port:
                  number: 80

Summary
Root causes were a label mismatch (app=web vs app=nginx) and wrong targetPort (80 vs 8080). I corrected the Service to select app=nginx and route port 80 to targetPort 8080. The Service now has healthy endpoints and should be accessible within the cluster. Let me know if you want me to expose it externally and by which method (NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress).

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found and fixed

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler could not place the pods (FailedScheduling).
- Service port mismatch: The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default, but the Service was targeting port 80. Traffic to web-app-service:80 was DNAT’d to pod:80 where nothing was listening, resulting in “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
  - Deployment: web-app-deployment (namespace: webshop-frontend)
- Corrected the Service to target the container’s actual port.
  - Service: web-app-service now has targetPort: 8080 (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), and a named port “http”.

Current status (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Endpoints: web-app-service now shows both pod IPs on port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl http://web-app-service returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Why the original error happened
- With the wrong targetPort, kube-proxy routed connections to pod:80. Since nothing was listening on 80 in the nginx-unprivileged container, the kernel returned RST, hence “connection refused.”
- Before fixing scheduling, there were also no runnable pods, so the Service would have had no endpoints at all.

Optional improvements (tell me if you want me to apply them)
- Align Deployment containerPort to 8080 and name it “http” for clarity.
- Add readiness and liveness probes (e.g., HTTP GET / on port 8080).
- If you truly need GPU/isolated nodes, add the environment=production-gpu label to appropriate nodes (or use tolerations/affinity as needed), then reintroduce a correct nodeSelector/affinity on the Deployment.

Let me know if you want me to proceed with the optional hardening changes.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what I found and fixed

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler could not place the pods (FailedScheduling).
- Service port mismatch: The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default, but the Service was targeting port 80. Traffic to web-app-service:80 was DNAT’d to pod:80 where nothing was listening, resulting in “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
  - Deployment: web-app-deployment (namespace: webshop-frontend)
- Corrected the Service to target the container’s actual port.
  - Service: web-app-service now has targetPort: 8080 (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), and a named port “http”.

Current status (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Endpoints: web-app-service now shows both pod IPs on port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl http://web-app-service returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Why the original error happened
- With the wrong targetPort, kube-proxy routed connections to pod:80. Since nothing was listening on 80 in the nginx-unprivileged container, the kernel returned RST, hence “connection refused.”
- Before fixing scheduling, there were also no runnable pods, so the Service would have had no endpoints at all.

Optional improvements (tell me if you want me to apply them)
- Align Deployment containerPort to 8080 and name it “http” for clarity.
- Add readiness and liveness probes (e.g., HTTP GET / on port 8080).
- If you truly need GPU/isolated nodes, add the environment=production-gpu label to appropriate nodes (or use tolerations/affinity as needed), then reintroduce a correct nodeSelector/affinity on the Deployment.

Let me know if you want me to proceed with the optional hardening changes.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found and fixed

Root causes
- Pods stuck Pending: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment: production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler could not place the pods (FailedScheduling).
- Service port mismatch: The container image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 by default, but the Service was targeting port 80. Traffic to web-app-service:80 was DNAT’d to pod:80 where nothing was listening, resulting in “connection refused”.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
  - Deployment: web-app-deployment (namespace: webshop-frontend)
- Corrected the Service to target the container’s actual port.
  - Service: web-app-service now has targetPort: 8080 (port 80 -> targetPort 8080), and a named port “http”.

Current status (verified)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Endpoints: web-app-service now shows both pod IPs on port 8080.
- In-pod test: curl http://web-app-service returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Why the original error happened
- With the wrong targetPort, kube-proxy routed connections to pod:80. Since nothing was listening on 80 in the nginx-unprivileged container, the kernel returned RST, hence “connection refused.”
- Before fixing scheduling, there were also no runnable pods, so the Service would have had no endpoints at all.

Optional improvements (tell me if you want me to apply them)
- Align Deployment containerPort to 8080 and name it “http” for clarity.
- Add readiness and liveness probes (e.g., HTTP GET / on port 8080).
- If you truly need GPU/isolated nodes, add the environment=production-gpu label to appropriate nodes (or use tolerations/affinity as needed), then reintroduce a correct nodeSelector/affinity on the Deployment.

Let me know if you want me to proceed with the optional hardening changes.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I’ve created the requested multi-tenant development setup. Summary of what’s been configured and applied:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for selection/isolation (env and tenant/shared labels)

RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace (least-privilege “edit”)
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User alice and SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User bob and SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User charlie and SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to shared namespace
  - dev-shared: RoleBinding dev-shared-view-developers -> ClusterRole view for Users alice, bob, charlie and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings created; only cluster-admins have access (implicit via existing ClusterRoleBinding)

Service Accounts
- Created per dev namespace:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod: limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny everywhere (non-system):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod (Ingress and Egress)
- Allow in-namespace communication:
  - allow-same-namespace in each of the above namespaces (Ingress and Egress within same namespace)
- Allow DNS egress from all namespaces:
  - allow-dns-egress targeting kube-system/coredns (k8s-app: kube-dns) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces can reach only dev-shared (not each other, nor staging/prod):
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector -> dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no traffic to/from dev namespaces

What this achieves
- Developers have full control in their own namespace; read-only visibility to dev-shared
- No developer access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; only allowed path is dev-<name> -> dev-shared
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev environments
- DNS works cluster-wide; other egress is denied by default (unless you later add policies)

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice            (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i create deploy --as alice              (no)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice                (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i create pods --as alice             (no)
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice                   (no)
- Network policies:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, reach a service/pod in dev-shared (should succeed)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From dev to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS lookups from any namespace (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your cluster’s authentication maps Users “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to the expected identities (OIDC, client certs, etc.) so the RoleBindings take effect.
- Service account tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - Get a short-lived token: kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others)
- DNS label caveat: The DNS policy targets pods labeled k8s-app=kube-dns in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels (e.g., coredns), adjust the selector accordingly.
- Optional hardening (recommended):
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits so quotas are always enforced even if developers omit them.
  - Consider Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted), seccomp, and NetworkPolicy egress rules for approved external destinations if internet access is needed.

If you want, I can also generate ready-to-commit YAML bundles (one per namespace) or add LimitRanges to complement the quotas.

  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User bob and SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User charlie and SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to shared namespace
  - dev-shared: RoleBinding dev-shared-view-developers -> ClusterRole view for Users alice, bob, charlie and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings created; only cluster-admins have access (implicit via existing ClusterRoleBinding)

Service Accounts
- Created per dev namespace:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod: limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny everywhere (non-system):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod (Ingress and Egress)
- Allow in-namespace communication:
  - allow-same-namespace in each of the above namespaces (Ingress and Egress within same namespace)
- Allow DNS egress from all namespaces:
  - allow-dns-egress targeting kube-system/coredns (k8s-app: kube-dns) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces can reach only dev-shared (not each other, nor staging/prod):
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector -> dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no traffic to/from dev namespaces

What this achieves
- Developers have full control in their own namespace; read-only visibility to dev-shared
- No developer access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; only allowed path is dev-<name> -> dev-shared
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev environments
- DNS works cluster-wide; other egress is denied by default (unless you later add policies)

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice            (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i create deploy --as alice              (no)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice                (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i create pods --as alice             (no)
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice                   (no)
- Network policies:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, reach a service/pod in dev-shared (should succeed)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From dev to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS lookups from any namespace (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your cluster’s authentication maps Users “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to the expected identities (OIDC, client certs, etc.) so the RoleBindings take effect.
- Service account tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - Get a short-lived token: kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others)
- DNS label caveat: The DNS policy targets pods labeled k8s-app=kube-dns in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels (e.g., coredns), adjust the selector accordingly.
- Optional hardening (recommended):
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits so quotas are always enforced even if developers omit them.
  - Consider Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted), seccomp, and NetworkPolicy egress rules for approved external destinations if internet access is needed.

If you want, I can also generate ready-to-commit YAML bundles (one per namespace) or add LimitRanges to complement the quotas.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I’ve created the requested multi-tenant development setup. Summary of what’s been configured and applied:

Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled for selection/isolation (env and tenant/shared labels)

RBAC
- Per-developer full access to their own namespace (least-privilege “edit”)
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding dev-alice-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User alice and SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding dev-bob-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User bob and SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding dev-charlie-edit -> ClusterRole edit for User charlie and SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Read-only access to shared namespace
  - dev-shared: RoleBinding dev-shared-view-developers -> ClusterRole view for Users alice, bob, charlie and their SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)
- Staging and prod: no developer bindings created; only cluster-admins have access (implicit via existing ClusterRoleBinding)

Service Accounts
- Created per dev namespace:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa

Resource Quotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie: limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging, prod: limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

Network Policies (isolation and least privilege)
- Default deny everywhere (non-system):
  - default-deny-all in dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod (Ingress and Egress)
- Allow in-namespace communication:
  - allow-same-namespace in each of the above namespaces (Ingress and Egress within same namespace)
- Allow DNS egress from all namespaces:
  - allow-dns-egress targeting kube-system/coredns (k8s-app: kube-dns) in each namespace
- Developer namespaces can reach only dev-shared (not each other, nor staging/prod):
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow-egress-to-dev-shared (namespaceSelector -> dev-shared)
  - In dev-shared: allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces (from namespaces dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress allowed; no traffic to/from dev namespaces

What this achieves
- Developers have full control in their own namespace; read-only visibility to dev-shared
- No developer access to staging/prod
- Cross-developer traffic is blocked; only allowed path is dev-<name> -> dev-shared
- Staging/prod are isolated from dev environments
- DNS works cluster-wide; other egress is denied by default (unless you later add policies)

How to verify quickly
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice auth can-i create deploy --as alice            (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-bob auth can-i create deploy --as alice              (no)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i get pods --as alice                (yes)
  - kubectl -n dev-shared auth can-i create pods --as alice             (no)
  - kubectl -n staging auth can-i get pods --as alice                   (no)
- Network policies:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, reach a service/pod in dev-shared (should succeed)
  - From dev-alice to dev-bob (should fail)
  - From dev to staging/prod (should fail)
  - DNS lookups from any namespace (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- User identities: Ensure your cluster’s authentication maps Users “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie” to the expected identities (OIDC, client certs, etc.) so the RoleBindings take effect.
- Service account tokens (K8s v1.24+):
  - Get a short-lived token: kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa (repeat for others)
- DNS label caveat: The DNS policy targets pods labeled k8s-app=kube-dns in kube-system. If your DNS deployment uses different labels (e.g., coredns), adjust the selector accordingly.
- Optional hardening (recommended):
  - Add LimitRanges in each namespace to set default requests/limits so quotas are always enforced even if developers omit them.
  - Consider Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted), seccomp, and NetworkPolicy egress rules for approved external destinations if internet access is needed.

If you want, I can also generate ready-to-commit YAML bundles (one per namespace) or add LimitRanges to complement the quotas.
